title: Grove's emergency protocol is composed from ordinary relayer functions; the only special power is revoking a relayer
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.3 collects "all the possible actions that can be taken in case of an emergency", and what is striking is that almost none of them are emergency-specific. A...3.2.1 calls `redeemERC4626(token, token.balanceOf(proxy))`; A...3.3 calls `swapUSDCToUSDS(usdc.balanceOf(proxy))`; A...3.4 calls `burnUSDS(usds.balanceOf(proxy))`. Each cross-references the routine procedure that defines it. The emergency is a **sequence and a set of arguments** — full balances instead of chosen amounts — not a separate code path.

The only genuinely privileged step is A...3.1: the `FREEZER_ROLE` calls `removeRelayer(compromisedRelayer)`, after which "the backstop relayer can then take over." A second relayer is pre-provisioned so that revocation does not leave Grove unable to act — freezing removes the compromised actor without removing the capability.

Designing it this way means the emergency path is exercised by every normal day of operation, so it cannot rot the way an unused break-glass mechanism does. It also means the emergency inherits every routine constraint, including rate limits — which is precisely why the unlimited outflow limits in the instance configurations are load-bearing rather than lax.

A...3.1 also narrows the freeze by policy beyond what the code enforces: it "should only be used if the keys to the relayer multisig have been leaked or compromised, and the relayer is now in the hands of an external bad actor." The Artifact restricts a capability the contract would otherwise permit for any reason — a governance constraint layered on a technical one.
description: The documented unwind — redeem all ERC-4626, swap USDC to USDS, burn USDS — uses the same functions as routine operation, with a pre-provisioned backstop relayer taking over after a freeze.
